But many approximations arrive one step at a time. Bisection gives a first interval, then a second, then a third. A decimal approximation gives a first decimal, then a second, then a third.

In your own words, what changes when the input is a counting number n=1,2,3,\ldots rather than a continuous variable x, and why do bisection and decimal approximations naturally produce sequences?

hint.p: The input no longer fills an interval; it arrives one step at a time. Nested intervals and longer decimals are lists indexed by whole numbers.

statement.p: This sequence does not settle down. It alternates forever.
Some sequences are not first given by an explicit formula. They are given by a starting value and a rule for the next term.
The terms move toward 2. Each step takes the current value and moves halfway from it to 2.
Recursive sequences will appear later in Newton’s method and Euler’s method. They are how a computer often follows a mathematical process step by step.

subsection.title: Monotone bounded sequences
subsection.p: Some sequences converge because they move steadily in one direction and cannot escape.
The decimal approximations
move upward toward \sqrt2. They never pass \sqrt2. They are increasing and bounded above.
This is a common pattern.

note.title: Monotone sequences
note.p: A sequence is monotone if it is increasing or decreasing.

subsection.p: Here “increasing” allows equality. Some books call this nondecreasing.

exercise.title: Why do monotone bounded sequences have to settle?

statement.p: The decimal approximations 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, \ldots increase and never pass \sqrt2. In your own words, why does an increasing sequence that is bounded above converge, and why is this one of the first places completeness of the real numbers is doing essential work?

hint.p: The set of terms has a least upper bound L. Increasing terms cannot jump over L, and they cannot stay a fixed distance below it forever. Completeness is what supplies that least upper bound.

This is why bisection is reliable. It does not guess wildly. It creates sequences that are forced to settle.

exercise.title: Why is an infinite sum secretly a sequence problem?

statement.p: We do not add infinitely many terms all at once. We add the first N terms and watch the partial sums as N\to\infty. In your own words, what does it mean for a series to converge, and how is bisection the same kind of settling?

hint.p: A series converges when its sequence of partial sums converges. Bisection creates nested endpoint sequences whose lengths shrink to zero, so those sequences are forced to settle to the trapped root.
